**Scratching** is playing the record as an instrument: moving it back and forth under the needle while the other hand opens and closes
the sound with a fader. Grand Wizzard Theodore is credited with discovering it in the Bronx in the late 1970s; Grandmaster Flash,
DJ Jazzy Jeff, Qbert and the turntablist crews made it an art.

## Set up

- **A short sound** at the start of a cue: "Ahh" or a horn stab. Put a cue point (or a sticker on the record) right at its start.
- **Record hand** on the label; it pushes the record forward and pulls it back.
- **Fader hand** on the crossfader or channel fader, with a **sharp curve**, so a tiny movement opens or closes the sound.
- One revolution of the record at 33⅓ RPM is 1.8 seconds of sound. Short scratches move the record a quarter turn or less.

Below: one deck with the scratch sample, and a mixer with its fader. Click **CUE** (stopped) at the start of the "Ahh" to mark it. The platter's
**label** is the record: drag it forwards and backwards. Use your other hand (or a second finger on a touch screen) on the channel **fader**.

<div class="dj-tt" data-id="dj-scratch" data-decks="1" data-a="demo:ahh" data-show="decks mixer library" data-curve="1"></div>

## The scratches

Learn each slowly, then in time with a beat (play a loop on your phone or the next widget's deck at 90 BPM).

1. **Baby scratch**: record hand only, fader open. Push forward a quarter turn, pull back, in steady eighth notes. Forward is the sound
   played; back is it reversed. Even, smooth movements; the sound should be the same each time.
2. **Forward scratch**: push forward with the fader **open**, close the fader, pull back silently, open it again. Only the forward sound is heard.
   (The opposite, sound only on the pull, is a backward scratch.)
3. **Chirp**: push forward and close the fader *during* the push; open it as you pull back and close it again during the pull. Each movement
   gets cut off, making a short "chirp". Record and fader hands move together.
4. **Transformer**: let the record move slowly (a slow push of a long "Ahh"), and tap the fader open and closed in rhythm, so the long sound
   is chopped into pulses (sixteenths, triplets). Named after the sound effects of the *Transformers* cartoon.

## Back on the beat

Scratches sit on a beat played by the other deck. Here deck A plays a boom-bap loop at 90 BPM; deck B has the "Ahh". With the crossfader curve
sharp, cut B in and out from the crossfader while scratching it.

<div class="dj-tt" data-id="dj-scratch2" data-a="demo:boom90" data-b="demo:ahh" data-curve="1" data-show="decks mixer library"></div>

## Hamster switch, tips

- Many scratch DJs reverse the crossfader direction (**hamster** style) so the fader hand pushes towards the deck being scratched.
- Keep the needle (here, the platter) steady: **small, precise movements** sound better than big ones.
- Practise slowly with a metronome; speed comes later.
